title: Gold Falls Sharply in Dollars, but Indian Gold ETFs Still Hold Gains Since Last Diwali
excerpt: Spot gold is down 28.8% from its January peak in dollar terms, yet a weaker rupee and higher import duty cushioned the rupee fall, and Indian gold ETFs averaged 9.22% since Diwali 2025.
body:
• Spot gold fell below $4,000 an ounce on October 30, closing at $3,982.03, down 28.8% in dollar terms from its January 29 peak of $5,595, according to spot and LBMA prices cited in a detailed market analysis.
  • Indian prices fell less: the IBJA benchmark for 999 gold closed at Rs 1,40,054 per 10 grams on October 30, and Nippon India ETF Gold BeES was down about 20.7% from its peak, cushioned by a weaker rupee and a higher import duty.
  • All 25 gold ETF schemes tracked by Dhan recorded negative returns over the past month as of November 4, with losses between 3.66% and 4.53%, according to a Livemint report cited by Angel One.
  • For a rupee investor the longer picture is different: gold ETFs delivered an average return of 9.22% since Diwali 2025, and the category was up 6.94% so far this year as of October 26, Value Research data cited by Livemint shows — the dollar fall is not the return an Indian holder actually earned.

Gold has fallen sharply in dollar terms this year, but the return an Indian investor has actually seen is smaller, because the rupee price of gold is built from three moving parts: the world dollar price, the rupee-dollar exchange rate, and India's import duty. Two of those three moved in the Indian buyer's favour this year and cushioned the fall.

What was reported

On Friday, October 30, spot gold fell 0.98% to $3,982.03 an ounce, after trading between $3,965 and $4,026, according to an analysis of IBJA, AMFI and LBMA data. Measured from the peak on January 29, gold was down 28.8% in dollars, from $5,595 to $3,982 an ounce. In India, the IBJA benchmark rate for 999 gold closed October 30 at Rs 1,40,054 per 10 grams, Rs 2,201 lower than the previous day. A separate market report cited by Angel One put domestic gold prices near Rs 1,42,000 per 10 grams, compared with an earlier peak of nearly Rs 1,80,000, a correction of more than 20%.

Why the rupee fall was smaller

The same analysis, using daily net asset values published by AMFI, measured Nippon India ETF Gold BeES down 19.4% from its January 29 peak of Rs 144.57 a unit to Rs 116.48 on October 29, and about 20.7% lower after October 30. The gap between the dollar fall and the rupee fall has two named causes. The rupee weakened from Rs 91.96 a dollar on January 29 to Rs 94.94 on October 23, according to FBIL rates cited in the analysis. Import duty rose from 6% to 15% on May 13, 2026, when a customs notification doubled the basic customs duty from 5% to 10%. Put together, the analysis calculates that a 28.8% dollar fall, combined with a 3.2% rupee move and an 8.5% duty effect, leaves the rupee price about 20% lower, close to what the Gold BeES net asset value shows.

What happened to gold ETFs

The correction reached fund returns in the past month. As per a Livemint report cited by Angel One, all 25 listed gold ETF schemes tracked by Dhan recorded negative returns over the past month as of November 4, 2026. Losses ranged between 3.66% and 4.53%: Zerodha Gold ETF declined 4.53%, followed by Mirae Asset Gold ETF at 4.47% and UTI Gold ETF at 4.41%.

Over a longer window, the same Livemint reporting shows a different result. Since Diwali 2025, which was celebrated on October 20, gold ETFs delivered an average return of 9.22% across 22 schemes. Nippon India Gold ETF BeES led with 12.58%, just ahead of Invesco Gold ETF at 12.50% and ICICI Gold ETF at 12.39%. Value Research data cited in the same report put the whole category up 6.94% so far this year, 18.64% over the past year, 31.90% over three years and 23.15% over five years, as of October 26, 2026. Those are reported past returns, not a forecast.

Why gold fell

Both reports point to the same drivers. A stronger US dollar, elevated interest rates and developments in West Asia contributed to the recent decline, according to news reports cited by Angel One. Higher interest rates increase the opportunity cost of holding gold, which does not generate interest income, and a stronger dollar makes bullion more expensive for buyers using other currencies. The market analysis adds that the Federal Reserve held its policy rate at 3.75% to 4% on October 28, after raising rates on September 16, and that two voting members wanted a further quarter-point rise.

What to watch next

Demand data offers context, not a price call. The World Gold Council's India report for July to September 2026, published on November 3 on Metals Focus data and summarised in the market analysis, put total Indian demand at 162.5 tonnes, down 29% from a year earlier, while gold ETFs took in 5.3 tonnes and holdings reached around 124 tonnes. The Council expects festive and wedding buying to lift the October to December quarter; that is an expectation, not a result. The same analysis flags a risk specific to India: what a duty rise added, a duty cut can take away. If duty returned from 15% to 6%, it calculates the Indian price would fall by about 7.8% at once, with no change in world prices. For diaspora investors holding Indian gold ETFs, the practical point is that their return is set by the dollar price, the rupee and Indian duty policy together, not by the headline dollar move alone.
